figures.shows: Log-log plot of estimated expected time (hours) and physical qubit count (megaqubits) (y, about 1 to 100000) against modulus length n (x, about 1024 to 65536 bits) for RSA via Ekera-Hastad (also with 0.01% gate error instead of 0.1%), short DLP or Schnorr DLP via Ekera-Hastad, Schnorr DLP via Shor, general DLP via Ekera-Hastad and general DLP via Shor; each series rises roughly as a power law with n, hours (solid) above megaqubits for the hardest cases, the lowest curves are about 1 to 2 at n about 1024 and the highest reach about 10000 to 20000 at n about 65536, with small jumps near n about 32768.
figures.confirmed_by: The jumps in space around n = 32786 occur as the algorithm exceeds the error budget of the CCZ factory from [36] and switches to the T factory from [27].

figures.shows: Working through the exponent qubits of Shor's algorithm with window size cexp = 4: groups of four qubits prepared in plus with Rz rotations, feeding a lookup input block e[ne-4:ne], then a QFT and measurement, followed by multiplication by g to the power 2^(ne-4) times the window value mod N; the pattern repeats for the next window.
figures.confirmed_by: This reduces the number of multiplications by a factor of the window size, at the cost of some additional lookup work within the multiplication.

figures.shows: How to temporarily reduce oblivious carry runways to a single qubit: register pieces register[0,csep), runway0, register[csep, csep+cpad) and so on, with Input r0 and Input r1 blocks, add and subtract of the runway values into cpad plus-state qubits, so each runway is reduced to one carry qubit before a multiply-add.
figures.confirmed_by: This temporarily reduces each runway to a single carry qubit (see Figure 3).

figures.shows: Space usage (rows of logical qubits, y) against time (x) during the lookup-add-unlookup inner loop, in stages Ready, Lookup, Addition, Unlookup, Ready; colour-coded rows for workspace, CCZ factory, CCZ fixup, target register, factor register, temp register, lookup workspace and MAJ/UMA sweep; the addition stage squeezes target and temp registers through a moving operating area.
figures.confirmed_by: Uncomputing the lookup is done with measurement-based uncomputation [8], which is overlapped slightly with the UMA sweep

figures.shows: Data layout during a parallel addition for n = 2048: a 225 by 63 logical qubit grid with unprocessed rows, rows of factories, a ripple carry strip, processed rows and idle data; the left and right halves (low and high half of the registers) run independently in parallel.
figures.confirmed_by: The left and right halves of the computer run completely independently and in parallel.

figures.shows: Data layout during a table lookup for n = 2048 on a 225 by 63 logical qubit grid: double access data rows, a unary iterate strip (dark gray), factories and idle data; every lookup output qubit is adjacent to two access hallways.
figures.confirmed_by: There are enough factories, and enough work space, to run the lookup at double speed

figures.shows: Spacetime layout (three-dimensional rendering; time upward, truncated) during part of an addition: red CCZ factory boxes, pink AutoCCZ fixup boxes, light blue MAJ boxes sweeping through yellow and green register rows, with dark blue idle register rows; to scale for n = 2048 with level 2 code distance 27 and level 1 code distance 17 on a 225 by 63 grid.
figures.confirmed_by: The diagram is to scale for n = 2048 with a level 2 code distance of d = 27 and a level 1 code distance of 17

figures.shows: Stabilizer configuration diagrams of lattice surgery qubits in the rotated surface code at code distances 3, 5 and 11: yellow data qubits, black and gray four-body Z and X stabilizers and black and gray two-body semi-circle stabilizers.
figures.confirmed_by: There are 2(d + 1)2 physical qubits per logical qubit, including the spacing between logical qubits.

figures.shows: A possible dense packing of idle qubits in the surface code (bulb shapes), one distance 13 logical qubit per bulb with red and blue lines marking its X and Z observables; uses 1.5 d squared plus O(d) physical qubits instead of 2(d+1) squared.
figures.confirmed_by: A possible dense packing for idle qubits, using 1.5d2 + O(d) physical qubits instead of 2(d + 1)2.

figures.shows: Expected costs of factoring n bit RSA integers by construction (Vedral 1996, Zalka 1998 variants, Beauregard 2002, Fowler 2012, Haner 2016, ours 2019) with abstract qubits, measurement depth, Toffoli+T/2 count (asymptotic and in billions at n = 1024, 2048, 3072) and minimum spacetime volume (megaqubitdays); ours: 0.4, 2.7 and 9.9 billion Toffoli+T/2 and 0.5, 5.9 and 21 megaqubitdays; one elliptic curve row (Roetteler 2017) at n = 160, 224, 256.
figures.confirmed_by: Compared to previous works, we reduce the Toffoli count when factoring RSA integers by over 10x (see Table 1).

figures.shows: Historical estimates for factoring n = 2048 bit RSA integers with their physical assumptions (gate error rate 0.1% to 0.2%, cycle time, reaction time, connectivity, distillation and execution strategy) and costs: Van Meter 2009 6500 million qubits, 410 days, 2600000 megaqubitdays; Jones 2010 620, 10, 6200; Fowler 2012 1000, 1.1, 1100; O'Gorman 2017 230, 3.7, 850; Gheorghiu 2019 170, 1, 170; ours 16, 6, 90 (1 factory); 19, 0.36, 6.6 (1 thread); 20, 0.31, 5.9 (parallel).
figures.confirmed_by: We improve on their estimates by over 100x (see Table 2) when accounting for slight remaining differences in the cost model.

figures.shows: Factoring an n bit RSA integer by computing a short discrete logarithm for n = 1024, 2048, 3072, 4096, 8192, 12288, 16384 with chosen parameters (d1, d2, delta_off, cmul, cexp, csep), retry risk, volume per run and expected (megaqubitdays), qubits (megaqubits) and runtime per run (hours); for n = 2048: d1 15, d2 27, retry risk 31%, 4.1 per run and 5.9 expected megaqubitdays, 20 megaqubits, 5.1 hours per run.

papers.what_it_is: A Google and KTH paper that combines windowed arithmetic, the coset representation, oblivious carry runways and an optimized surface-code spacetime layout to estimate that 2048 bit RSA could be factored in about 8 hours with about 20 million noisy superconducting qubits, and extends the estimates to finite-field discrete logarithms.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in Shor's original algorithm, period finding is performed on f(e) = g to the power e and involves a modular exponentiation with ne = 2n qubits in the exponent, and that r is even with g to the power r/2 not equal to minus 1 with probability at least 1/2 by Shor's paper.

which holds with probability at least 1/2 by [79]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Shor [79].

assertions.value: The authors state that in the Ekera-Hastad algorithm the total exponent length is ne = 3m = 1.5n + O(1) qubits, compared to 2n qubits in Shor's algorithm, with m = 0.5n + O(1).
quotes: We set m = 0.5n + O(1).
The total exponent length is hence ne = 3m = 1.5n + O(1) qubits, compared to 2n qubits in Shor's algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: A property of the Ekera-Hastad algorithm that the paper takes from references [21, 23, 25].

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ekera, that the classical post-processing algorithm of the Ekera-Hastad method has probability above 99% of recovering d, so in general it suffices to run the quantum algorithm once.

this implies that it in general suffices to run the quantum algorithm once.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to reference [23].

assertions.value: The authors state that the reference implementation, built from controlled modular multiplications, has a Toffoli count of ne times 2n times 5 times 2n, which is 20 ne n squared, and that it is the baseline for the optimizations.
quotes: Combining the numbers in the preceding two paragraphs implies a Toffoli count of ne·2n·5·2n = 20nen2 for the reference implementation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting argument from assumed per-addition costs (a Cuccaro adder with 2n Toffolis and five additions per modular addition).

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum Fourier transform can be implemented semi-classically and interleaved with the controlled modular multiplications, so that its cost is negligible, and that success probabilities are analyzed assuming an ideal QFT.
quotes: This implies that the cost of implementing the QFT is negligible.
we assume the use of an ideal QFT even though the implemented QFT is technically an approximation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its cost analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that switching to the coset representation of modular integers lets a controlled non-modular addition cost 4n Toffolis instead of the 10n assumed for a controlled modular adder, reducing the leading Toffoli term of the reference implementation from 20 ne n squared to 8 ne n squared.
quotes: It is possible to perform a controlled non-modular addition in 4n Toffolis [18, 32], significantly cheaper than the 10n we assumed for a controlled modular adder.
Therefore switching to the coset representation reduces the leading asymptotic term of the Toffoli count of the reference implementation from 20nen2 to 8nen2.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting argument with the padding cost treated as logarithmic and small.

assertions.value: The authors state that the periodicity of the coset superposition lets a non-modular adder perform approximate modular addition, that the error can be exponentially suppressed by adding more padding, and that the padding required is logarithmic in the number of operations.
quotes: the periodicity of the superposition causes a non-modular adder to perform approximate modular addition on this representation, and the error of the approximation can be exponentially suppressed by adding more padding to the register.
the amount of padding required is logarithmic in the number of operations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in prose with the formal analysis cited to reference [33].

assertions.value: The authors state that they estimate the probabilities of topological, approximation, magic state distillation and classical post-processing errors, combine them assuming independence into an upper bound on the overall probability of error, and choose the parameters that minimize the skewed expected spacetime volume.

papers.what_it_is: A Google Quantum AI, Columbia and Macquarie paper that block encodes the tensor hypercontraction (THC) electronic Hamiltonian in a larger non-orthogonal diagonal basis, qubitizes it with O(N lambda over epsilon) Toffoli complexity, corrects earlier resource estimates of other qubitization methods, and lays out a FeMoCo computation in the surface code.

assertions.value: The authors state that they describe quantum circuits with only O(N) Toffoli complexity that block encode the spectra of quantum chemistry Hamiltonians in a basis of N arbitrary (for example molecular) orbitals.
quotes: We describe quantum circuits with only O(N ) Toffoli complexity that block encode the spectra of quantum chemistry Hamiltonians in a basis of N arbitrary (e.g., molecular) orbitals.
assertions.certainty_reason: An abstract statement of the per-step cost; the full cost needs the repetition count (next assertion).

assertions.value: The authors state that with O(lambda over epsilon) repetitions of these circuits one can use phase estimation to sample in the molecular eigenbasis, where lambda is the 1-norm of the Hamiltonian coefficients and epsilon is the target precision.
quotes: With O(λ/ ) repetitions of these circuits one can use phase estimation to sample in the molecular eigenbasis, where λ is the 1-norm of Hamiltonian coefficients
assertions.certainty_reason: An author result under the paper's stated assumptions.
assertions.reader_inference: The total Toffoli cost is O(N lambda over epsilon): the per-step O(N) times the O(lambda over epsilon) repetitions.

assertions.value: The authors claim that this is the lowest complexity that has been shown for quantum computations of chemistry within an arbitrary basis and that, up to logarithmic factors, it matches the scaling of the most efficient prior block encodings that work only with orthogonal basis functions diagonalizing the Coulomb operator, such as the plane wave dual basis.
quotes: This is the lowest complexity that has been shown for quantum computations of chemistry within an arbitrary basis.
this matches the scaling of the most efficient prior block encodings that can only work with orthogonal basis functions diagonalizing the Coloumb operator
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim or judgement without a separate proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that their key insight is to factorize the Hamiltonian by tensor hypercontraction (THC) and transform the Coulomb operator into an isospectral diagonal form in a non-orthogonal basis defined by the THC factors, and then to use qubitization on it.
quotes: Our key insight is to factorize the Hamiltonian using a method known as tensor hypercontraction (THC) and then to transform the Coulomb operator into an isospectral diagonal form with a
non-orthogonal basis defined by the THC factors.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the method the paper analyzes.

assertions.value: The authors state that compilation of their algorithm for finite-sized molecules such as FeMoCo reveals that the method requires the least fault-tolerant resources of any known approach.
quotes: compilation of our algorithm for challenging finite-sized molecules such as FeMoCo reveals that our method requires the least fault-tolerant resources of any known approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison across methods under the paper's own accounting (Table III).

assertions.value: The authors state that, by laying out and optimizing the surface code resources, FeMoCo can be simulated using about four million physical qubits and under four days of runtime, assuming 1 microsecond cycle times and physical gate error rates no worse than 0.1%.
quotes: we show that FeMoCo can be simulated using about four million physical qubits and under four days of runtime, assuming 1 μs cycle times and physical gate error rates no worse than 0.1%.
assertions.certainty_reason: A resource estimate from a surface code layout, not a run.
assertions.reader_inference: The estimate is for the Reiher active space; the more accurate Li Hamiltonian is not laid out in the surface code.

assertions.value: The authors state that the holy grail of quantum chemistry is a generally applicable electronic structure method that yields relative energies with errors less than 1.6 milliHartrees, called chemical accuracy, which is still a long-standing challenge.
quotes: relative energies with errors less than 1.6 milliHartrees
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the accuracy target it uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that the work of Reiher et al., using a Trotter-based approach, required more than 1014 (ten to the fourteenth, printed flat) T gates to simulate an active space model of FeMoCo.
quotes: The work of Reiher et al. required more than 1014 T gates to simulate an active space model of FeMoCo.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that distilling the magic states needed for the Reiher et al. FeMoCo calculation alone would require four million qubitdecades, given roughly 15 qubitseconds of spacetime volume per T gate.

papers.what_it_is: An IBM Research paper that proposes amplitude-estimation algorithms for expected value, variance, VaR and CVaR, with a trade-off between circuit depth and convergence rate, a 5-qubit hardware demonstration and noisy simulations of a two-asset Treasury portfolio.

assertions.value: The authors state that they employ quantum amplitude estimation to evaluate risk measures such as Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk on a gate-based quantum computer.
quotes: We employ quantum amplitude estimation to evaluate risk measures such as Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk on a gate-based quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the scope of the paper's own method.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical Monte Carlo simulations converge at a rate of O(M to the power minus 1/2) in the number of samples M.
quotes: This is already faster than classical Monte Carlo simulations which converge at a rate of O(M −1/2).
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement that the paper attributes to the Monte Carlo literature (reference [1]).

assertions.value: The authors state that the shortest possible circuit depth, growing polynomially in the number of qubits representing the uncertainty, leads to a convergence rate of O(M to the power minus 2/3).
quotes: The shortest possible circuit depth - growing polynomially in the number of qubits representing the uncertainty - leads to a convergence rate of O(M −2/3).
assertions.certainty_reason: The result is derived with a first-order Taylor argument that drops higher-order terms (Eq. 10).
assertions.reader_inference: The 2/3 rate holds only for the Taylor-approximated rotation (u = 0) and ignores higher-order terms and the number of repeated shots.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the circuit depth is allowed to grow faster, but still polynomially, the convergence rate quickly approaches the optimum of O(M to the power minus 1).
quotes: For increasing u, the convergence rate quickly approaches the optimal rate of O M −1 .
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from the approximate error bound of Eq. 12 with higher-order terms ignored.

assertions.value: The authors state that amplitude estimation returns an integer y, classically mapped to the estimator a-tilde = sin squared of (y pi over M), which satisfies an error bound of order pi over M plus pi squared over M squared, which is O(M to the power minus 1), with probability of at least 8 over pi squared.
quotes: This results in an integer y ∈ {0, ..., M − 1}, which is classically mapped to the estimator a ̃ = sin2(yπ/M ) ∈ [0, 1].
≤ π M + π2 M2 = O M −1 , (2) with probability of at least 8 π2 .
assertions.certainty_reason: The bound is taken from Brassard, Hoyer, Mosca and Tapp (reference [8]), not proved in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that amplitude estimation requires m additional qubits and M equal to 2 to the power m applications of the operator Q.
quotes: This requires m additional qubits and M = 2m applications of Q.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the resource count of the algorithm it builds on, in its own setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that choosing f(i) = i/(N - 1) allows amplitude estimation to estimate E[X/(N - 1)] and hence E[X].
quotes: allows us to estimate E[ X N −1 ] and hence E[X].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper cites this construction from earlier work (references [15, 16]).

assertions.value: The authors state that choosing f(i) = i squared over (N - 1) squared lets them estimate E[X squared], which yields the variance Var(X) = E[X squared] - E[X] squared.
quotes: If we choose f (i) = i2/(N − 1)2 we can efficiently estimate E[X2] which yields the variance Var(X) = E[X2] − E[X]2.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction stated without a separate proof.

assertions.value: The paper defines VaR at confidence level alpha, for alpha in [0, 1], as the smallest value x in {0, ..., N - 1} such that P[X <= x] >= (1 - alpha).
quotes: For a given confidence level α ∈ [0, 1], VaRα(X) can be defined as the smallest value x ∈ {0, ..., N − 1} such that P[X ≤ x] ≥ (1 − α).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines VaR for its own algorithm in Section II.
assertions.reader_inference: Section III writes the same search condition as P[X <= l_alpha] >= alpha, which differs from this definition by 1 - alpha versus alpha.

assertions.value: The authors state that a bisection search over the level l finds the smallest l_alpha such that P[X <= l_alpha] >= 1 - alpha in at most n steps, and that VaR is then estimated with accuracy O(M to the power minus 1), a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods.
quotes: with a bisection search over l we can find the smallest level lα such that P[X ≤ lα] ≥ 1 − α in at most n steps.
This allows us to estimate VaRα(X) as before with accuracy O M −1 , which again is a quadratic speedup compared to classical Monte Carlo methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a full proof; each bisection step needs a separate amplitude estimation, a cost the paper does not count.
assertions.reader_inference: The accuracy and speedup statement is per amplitude estimation call; the bisection multiplies the number of calls by up to n.

assertions.value: The authors describe Value at risk as a quantile of the loss distribution that is a widely used risk metric.
quotes: Value at risk (VaR) [1], a quantile of the loss distribution, is a widely used risk metric.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of background.

assertions.value: The authors define conditional value at risk as the expected loss for losses greater than VaR and state that, by contrast to VaR, CVaR is more sensitive to extreme events in the tail of the loss distribution.
quotes: defined as the expected loss for losses greater than VaR.
By contrast to VaR, CVaR is more sensitive to extreme events in the tail of the loss distribution.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the term it then uses.
assertions.reader_inference: Section II then computes CVaR as the conditional expectation restricted to {0, ..., l_alpha}, the lower tail of the variable, which is the tail that holds the loss in this paper's sign convention.

assertions.value: The authors state that CVaR at level alpha is the conditional expectation of X restricted to {0, ..., l_alpha}, with l_alpha computed as VaR.
quotes: CVaRα(X) is the conditional expectation of X re- stricted to {0, ..., lα}, where we compute lα = VaRα(X) as before.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction stated by the authors; the normalization uses an estimated probability.

assertions.value: The authors state, from a first-order Taylor bound in which higher order terms are omitted, that the quantum estimation of CVaR also achieves a quadratic speedup compared to classical Monte Carlo methods.
quotes: where again we omit higher order terms.
Thus, the quantum estimation of CVaR also achieves a quadratic speedup compared to classical Monte Carlo methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: The bound ignores higher-order terms (Appendix C), so it is an approximate result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the best known upper bound for the number of gates needed to create the state representing the distribution is O(2 to the power n) in general, and that approximations with polynomial complexity in n are possible for many distributions, for example log-concave distributions.
quotes: In general, the best known upper bound for the number of gates required to create |ψ n is O(2n) [17].
However, approximations with polynomial complexity in n are possible for many distributions, e.g., log-concave distributions [18].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to references [17] and [18].

assertions.value: The authors state that, in the remainder of Section III, they assume a given operator R such that R acting on the all-zero state of n qubits gives the state representing the distribution of X, so the cost of loading the distribution is not counted.
quotes: In the remainder of this section, we assume a given operator R such that R |0 n = |ψ n.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own gate counts.
assertions.reader_inference: Gate counts and speedups in Section III therefore exclude the cost of loading the distribution.

assertions.value: The authors state that representing the operator F for the expected value or for CVaR in general either requires an exponential O(2 to the power n) number of gates or additional ancillas to pre-compute the discretized function into qubits using quantum arithmetic.
quotes: In general, representing F for the expected value or for the CVaR either requires an exponential O(2n) number of gates or additional ancillas to pre-compute the (discretized) function f into qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement without proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that they approximate the operator F without ancillas using polynomially many gates, at the cost of a lower, but still faster than classical, rate of convergence.
quotes: approximating F without ancillas using polynomially many gates, at the cost of a lower - but still faster than classical - rate of convergence.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author summary of the method; the supporting bounds drop higher-order terms.
assertions.reader_inference: The next paragraph builds the rotation operator with O(n) ancillas for multi-controlled gates, so 'without ancillas' means without ancillas for pre-computing f, not none at all.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since the binary variable representation of the polynomial leads to at most n to the power k terms, the operator P can be constructed using O(n to the power k+1) gates and O(n) ancillas.
quotes: leads to at most nk terms, the operator P can be constructed using O(nk+1) gates and O(n) ancillas.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting argument in prose with a simplifying choice of O(n) gates and O(n) ancillas per multi-controlled gate.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Taylor approximation of order 2u + 1 leads to a maximal approximation error for Eq. 8 of c to the power 2u+3 over (2u + 3) times 2 to the power 2u+1, plus O(c to the power 2u+5),, as shown in Appendix B.
assertions.anchor: Section III, p.3; Appendix B, p.9
quotes: The Taylor approximation of order 2u + 1 leads to a maximal approximation error for Eq. (8) of
assertions.certainty_reason: The bound uses a bound on the next Taylor coefficient and ignores higher-order terms (Appendix B).

assertions.value: The authors state that for the resulting polynomial p(f(x)) of order s(2u + 1), the number of gates required to construct the circuit scales as O(n to the power s(2u+1)+1).
quotes: The number of gates required to construct the corresponding circuit scales as O ns(2u+1)+1 .
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows by substitution in the O(n to the power k+1) count; not separately proved.

assertions.value: The authors state that the smallest scenario of interest is s = 1 and u = 0, where both f and p are linear functions, and that the number of gates for F then scales quadratically as the number of qubits n grows linearly.
quotes: The smallest scenario of interest is s = 1 and u = 0, i.e., both, f and p, are linear functions
scales quadrati- cally as the number of qubits n representing |ψ n grows linearly.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the gate count formula; not separately proved.

assertions.value: The authors state that translating the error equation into a rate gives an estimation error of O(M to the power minus (2u+2)/(2u+3)), that for u = 0 this is O(M to the power minus 2/3), already better than the classical O(M to the power minus 1/2).
quotes: For u = 0, we get O M − 2 3 , which is already better than the classical convergence rate of O M − 1 2 .
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived by ignoring higher-order terms in Eq. 10 and optimizing the scaling parameter c.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup is counted in the number of amplitude estimation samples M, not in wall clock time, and ignores that the circuit depth grows with M.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the variance they apply the same idea with sin squared of y approximately y squared, and that the resulting convergence rate is again O(M to the power minus (2u+2)/(2u+3)).
quotes: The resulting con- vergence rate is again equal to O M− 2u+2 2u+3 .
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by analogy with the expected value, without a separate derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that with (n + 1) ancillas, adder circuits can construct the operator F_l for VaR using O(n) gates, and that the resulting convergence rate is O(M to the power minus 1).
quotes: With (n + 1) ancillas, adder-circuits can be used to construct Fl using O(n) gates [21], and the resulting convergence rate is O M −1 .
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated with a citation to the adder circuits of reference [21] and no separate proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that amplitude estimation can approximate CVaR with the same trade-off between circuit depth and convergence rate as for the expected value.
quotes: amplitude estimation can then be used to approximate CVaRα(X) with the same trade-off between circuit depth and convergence rate as for the expected value.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as following from the preceding discussion.

assertions.value: The authors describe a one-period binomial tree T-bill model in which a market participant expects a 0.25 percentage-point increase of the Federal Funds Rate with a 70% probability and no change with a 30% probability.
quotes: expects a δr = 0.25%-points increase of the Federal Funds Rate with a (1 − p) = 70% probability and no change with a p = 30% probability
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup of its first model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the T-bill experiment ran amplitude estimation with m = 1, 2, 3, 4 evaluation qubits, corresponding to M = 2, 4, 8, 16 samples, on the IBM Q 5 Yorktown (ibmqx2) quantum processor, at most five qubits.
quotes: qubits m = 1, 2, 3, 4 corresponding to M = 2, 4, 8, 16 samples, respectively, to estimate p = [X].
This requires at most five qubits and can be implemented and run on the IBM Q 5 Yorktown (ibmqx2) quantum processor
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup of its hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that each circuit was repeated 8192 times, the maximal number of shots in the IBM Q Experience, and that this constant overhead is ignored in the comparison of the algorithms.
quotes: Thus, we repeat every circuit 8192 times (i.e., the maximal number of shots in the IBM Q Experience) to get a reliable estimate.
This implies a constant overhead, which we ignore in the comparison of the algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: The hardware comparison with Monte Carlo counts samples M, not the 8192 shots per circuit, so it is not a comparison of total runtime or total circuit executions.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum algorithm outperforms the Monte Carlo method already for M = 16 samples (m = 4 evaluation qubits), the largest scenario run on real hardware.
quotes: The quantum algorithm presented in this paper outperforms the Monte Carlo method already for M = 16 samples (i.e. m = 4 evaluation qubits), which is the largest scenario we performed on the real hardware, see Fig. 5.
assertions.certainty_reason: One small experiment on a single device; the error bound used for the quantum side is built from the most probable result.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against an optimistic Monte Carlo bound with exact standard error and counts samples, not shots.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the hardware results the most frequent estimator approaches the real value p and the resolution of the algorithm increases with m.
quotes: it can be seen that the most frequent estimator approaches the real value p and how the resolution of the algorithm increases with m.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single hardware experiment on a 5-qubit device.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 4: for m = 4 on real hardware the most frequent estimate lies at about 0.3, next to the target value of 30% (red dashed line), with a frequency of about 0.15 on the panel axis, while for the smallest case the possible estimates sit at about 0.0 and about 1.0, far from the target.

it holds that θa ∈ [(y − 1)π/M, (y + 1)π/M ].

assertions.value: The authors report that a principal component analysis of the daily changes in the CMT rates finds that the first three principal components, named shift, twist and butterfly, account for 96% of the variance, and that the correlation coefficient between shift and twist is -1%.
quotes: A principal component analysis reveals that the first three principal components, named shift, twist and butterfly account for 96% of the variance
The correlation coefficient between shift and twist is −1%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one data set of historical rates.

assertions.value: The authors state that the demonstration uses face values of VF1 = VF2 = $100, initial yields r1,0 = 1.8% and r2,0 = 2.25% and a coupon rate c = 2.5% for the two-asset portfolio of a one-year bill and a two-year note.
quotes: For our demonstration we set VF1 = VF2 = $100, r1,0 = 1.8%, r2,0 = 2.25%, and c = 2.5% in Eq. (14).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the parameters of its own simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that three qubits represent the distribution of the shift S (eight values) and two qubits the distribution of the twist T (four values), with more qubits for S because the shift explains a larger part of the variance, and that only the first two principal components are kept.
quotes: We use three qubits, denoted by q0, q1, q2, to represent the distribution of S, and two, denoted by q3, q4, for
We use more qubits for S than for T since the shift explains a larger part of the variance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup of its own simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that, given the almost perfect symmetry of the historical data, they fit symmetric discrete distributions to the shift and the twist separately, assuming the two to be independent.
assertions.anchor: Section V, p.6; Section V.A, p.7
quotes: We thus assume them to be independent and fit discrete distributions to each separately, see Fig. 8.
Given the almost perfect symmetry of the historical data we fit symmetric distributions to it.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the modeling assumptions of its own simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: A correlation of -1% rules out only linear dependence, not other dependence between shift and twist.

assertions.value: The authors state that for simplicity they use a first order approximation of the portfolio value, which corresponds to studying the portfolio from the point of view of its duration, and that higher order expansions such as convexity could be considered at the cost of increased circuit depth.
quotes: For simplicity, we use a first order approximation
corresponds to studying the portfolio from the point of view of its duration [35].
Higher order expansions, e.g. convexity could be considered at the cost of increased circuit depth.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a number of samples set by m the two-asset portfolio simulation needs a total of m + 12 qubits for expected value and VaR and m + 13 qubits for CVaR.
quotes: we need a total of m+12 qubits for expected value and VaR, and m + 13 qubits for CVaR.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the resource count of its own simulated circuit.

assertions.value: The authors report that the exact 95% VaR level of $0.288 corresponds to 0.093 after the mapping, and that with m = 5 sample qubits the difference between the classical and the quantum estimate is 9%.
quotes: We compare the quantum estimation of risk to the exact 95% VaR level of $0.288.
With m = 5 sample qubits the difference between the classical and quantum estimates is 9%.
this classical VaR corresponds to 0.093
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation of one toy two-asset portfolio on an ideal quantum computer.

assertions.value: The authors report that the number of CNOT gates needed to calculate VaR approximately doubles each time a sample qubit is added, so it scales as O(M) with a resulting error of O(M to the power minus 1).
quotes: The number of CNOT gates needed to calculate VaR approximately doubles each time a sample qubit is added, see Tab. I, i.e. it scales as O(M ) with a resulting error of O(M −1).
assertions.certainty_reason: A count from simulated circuits for one toy model over five values of m.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table I that the number of CNOT gates to estimate VaR rises from 795 (m = 1) to 22'235 (m = 5) with all-to-all connectivity, and from 1'817 to 55'520 with IBM Q 20 connectivity, an overhead of 2.29 to 2.50.
assertions.certainty_reason: Gate counts from one compilation (QISKit 0.5) of one toy model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the connectivity of the IBM Q 20 chip increases the number of CNOT gates by a factor 2.5 compared with a chip with all-to-all connectivity, based on QISKit 0.5, and that future versions might further reduce the overhead.
quotes: We find that the connectivity of the IBM Q 20 chip increases the number of CNOT gates by a factor 2.5 when compared to a chip with all-to-all connectivity [51].
These results are based on QISKit 0.5, future version might be able to further reduce the CNOT overhead
assertions.certainty_reason: A compiler result for one toy circuit with one software version.

assertions.value: The authors state that energy relaxation is simulated with a rate gamma such that after a time t each qubit relaxes to the zero state with probability 1 - exp(-gamma t), that CNOT gates last 100 ns, that single qubit gates are instant and exempt from errors, and that cross-talk is included by a ZZ term with strength alpha in the CNOT generator.
quotes: Energy relaxation is simulated using a relaxation rate γ such that after a time t each qubit has a probability 1 − exp(−γt) of relaxing to |0
We set the duration of the CNOT gates to 100 ns and assume that the single qubit gates are done instantly and are thus exempt from errors.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own noise model.
assertions.reader_inference: Measurement error, unitary gate errors and single-qubit gate errors are outside the model.

quotes: The algorithm is successful if it manages to identify 0.5 with a probability greater than 50%.
despite the 4383 gates needed.
This simulation is run with m = 2 sample qubits
With our error model this is achieved for relaxation rates rγ < 10−4 s−1 and cross-talk strength |α| < 1%
assertions.certainty_reason: A noisy simulation of one toy model with a simple error model.

assertions.value: The authors state that a generous estimation of current hardware capabilities, with gamma = 10 to the power minus 4 per second (loosely based on T1 = 100 microseconds) and alpha = -2%, indicates that this simulation may be possible in the near future as long as other error sources are kept under control.
quotes: A generous estimation of current hardware capabilities with γ = 10−4 s−1 (loosely based on T1 = 100 μs) and α = −2%
indicates that this simulation may be possible in the near future as long as other error sources
assertions.certainty_reason: An author estimate of hardware capability in 2018.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 10(b): the frequency of measuring 0.5 falls from about 100 percent at the lowest relaxation rates to about 55 percent near the red line at a relaxation rate of about 10000 per second, and to about 0 percent for rates above about 100000000 per second; Figure 10(c) shows about 50 percent at cross-talk strength about -2.0 percent, rising to about 100 percent at about 0.0 percent.
quotes: This figure shows how the probability of measuring 0.5 decreases with increasing noise
The dashed red lines indicate the estimated state of the currently available hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they developed a quantum algorithm to estimate risk, resulting in a quadratic speedup compared to classical Monte Carlo methods, demonstrated on real hardware for a small model and studied for scalability and noise with a more complex simulated model.
quotes: We developed a quantum algorithm to estimate risk, e.g. for portfolios of financial assets, resulting in a quadratic speedup compared to classical Monte Carlo methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; the quadratic rate needs circuit depth that grows with M.

assertions.value: The authors state that, although the quadratic speedup can already be observed for a small number of samples, more is needed to achieve a practical quantum advantage, and that Monte Carlo simulations can be massively parallelized, which pushes the border for a quantum advantage even higher.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to calculate VaR for the two-asset portfolio on real quantum hardware, qubit coherence times will likely have to be increased by several orders of magnitude and cross-talk further suppressed.
quotes: on real quantum hardware it is likely that qubit coherence times will have to be increased by several orders of magnitude and that cross-talk will have to be further suppressed.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a limit of current hardware for its own calculation.

assertions.value: The authors state that loading random distributions or stochastic processes has been only briefly addressed, that it can be rather costly for auto-correlated processes, and that it needs to be further investigated.
quotes: For auto-correlated processes this can be rather costly and needs to be further investigated.

papers.what_it_is: A Goldman Sachs and IBM paper that gives end-to-end fault-tolerant resource estimates (logical qubits, T-count, T-depth) for pricing a basket autocallable and a TARF by amplitude estimation, introducing a re-parameterization method that loads paths with pre-trained variational Gaussian circuits.

papers.what_it_is: A Google Quantum AI perspective that uses back-of-the-envelope surface-code cost estimates to argue that quadratic quantum speedups will not give a runtime advantage on early fault-tolerant devices, while quartic speedups look practical.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that quadratic speedups will not enable quantum advantage on early generations of fault-tolerant devices unless there is a significant improvement in how quantum error-correction is realized.
quotes: We conclude that quadratic speedups will not enable quantum advantage on early generations of such fault-tolerant devices unless there is a significant improvement in how we would realize quantum error-correction.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion from a back-of-the-envelope model with stated assumptions, not a proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion is about runtime against a parallel classical adversary under the surface-code cost model of this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the conclusion persists even if the rate of logical gates in the surface code were increased by more than an order of magnitude.
quotes: While this conclusion persists even if we were to increase the rate of logical gates in the surface code by more than an order of magnitude
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement supported by the Table II estimates under the paper's assumptions.

assertions.value: The authors state that, repeating the analysis for speedups of other polynomial degrees, quartic speedups look significantly more practical.
quotes: we also repeat this analysis for speedups by other polynomial degrees and find that quartic speedups look significantly more practical.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion from the model estimates of Table I.

assertions.value: The authors state that a surface code Toffoli factory requires spacetime volume greater than ten qubitseconds under reasonable assumptions on an error-corrected superconducting qubit platform, while a classical nand circuit in CMOS runs with a few transistors in well under a nanosecond, roughly a ten order of magnitude difference.
quotes: requires spacetime volume greater than ten qubitseconds under reasonable assumptions on the capabilities of an error-corrected superconducting qubit platform [13].
Thus, there is roughly a ten order of magnitude difference between the spacetime volume required for comparable operations on an error-corrected quantum computer and a classical computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: An order-of-magnitude comparison from an estimate cited to reference [13].

assertions.value: The authors state that the central issue is that quantum error-correction and device operation time introduce significant constant factor slowdowns to the algorithm runtime.
quotes: The central issue is that quantum error-correction and device operation time introduce significant constant factor slowdowns to the algorithm runtime
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that for applications with an exponential speedup the exponential scaling of the classical approach quickly catches up to the large constant factors of the quantum approach, so a practical runtime advantage is possible even for modest problem sizes.
quotes: the exponential scaling of the classical approach quickly catches up to the large constant factors of the quantum approach
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement supported by cited resource-estimate studies.

assertions.value: The authors state that they focus on a modest realization of the surface code with enough resources to perform classically intractable calculations but only a few state distillation factories, and that the analysis uses current surface code projections.
quotes: We will focus on a modest realization of the surface code that would involve enough resources to perform classically intractable calculations but only support a few state distillation factories.

assertions.value: The authors assume a problem solvable by a classical computer making M to the power d calls to a classical primitive circuit or by a quantum computer making M calls to a quantum primitive circuit, which corresponds to an order d polynomial quantum speedup in the number of queries.

quotes: This generously assumes no prefactor overhead in a quantum implementation of an algorithm with respect to the number of calls required and along with other crude assumptions, allows us to bound the crossover time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states an assumption of its own model.
assertions.reader_inference: Because the assumptions favor the quantum side, the crossover times are lower bounds on the true crossover times under this cost model.

assertions.value: The authors state that their back-of-the-envelope analysis makes many assumptions overly optimistic towards the quantum computer and that they still conclude the prospects look poor for quadratic speedups with current error-correcting codes and architectures to outperform classical computers in time-to-solution.
